entities.name: Ezekiel
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Ezekiel, a pivotal figure in ancient Judeo-Christian literature, emerged during a tumultuous period of Israel's history. His prophetic ministry, active from 593 to 571 BC while in exile in Babylon, coincided with the destruction of Jerusalem and the First Temple. Ezekiel's visions and messages addressed the Jewish exiles, calling for repentance and offering hope for restoration. His profound influence is marked by his unique theological insights and vivid imagery, which have resonated through centuries of religious thought and interpretation.

The Book of Ezekiel records a series of remarkable visions, including the famous vision of the valley of dry bones, symbolizing the revival of the nation of Israel. Through his prophetic utterances, Ezekiel communicated God's judgment on Israel for its idolatry and social injustices, while also portraying a future restoration of the people and the Temple. One significant event was the prophetic vision of God's glory departing from the Temple, reflecting the dire state of Israel at that time. His writings, characterized by symbolic language and complex metaphors, fostered a rich theological tradition that continues to be studied and revered.

Ezekiel's legacy has profoundly shaped Jewish and Christian eschatology. His themes of judgment and restoration have influenced countless theologians, artists, and writers throughout history. The imagery and concepts found in his prophecies laid the groundwork for later apocalyptic literature, including the Book of Revelation in the New Testament. Furthermore, his call for social justice and ethical living resonates in contemporary discussions of faith and morality, illustrating the enduring relevance of his message.

entities.summary: Prophetic visions from Babylonian exile including the throne-chariot (ch. 1), the valley of dry bones (ch. 37), and the new Temple (chs. 40–48). Profoundly influenced Jewish mysticism (Merkabah) and Christian eschatology.
